summary: Averaged across all of Earth’s land, rainfall has not detectably changed in 26 years. Yet beneath that flat average, 9.9 million km² of land, an area the size of the United States, is getting significantly wetter or drier. Water decisions are made regionally, but no accessible tool shows where change is concentrated or how far to trust it. We developed Paradox Earth, an open pipeline and interactive 3D globe that tests 17,284 land regions in NASA GLDAS-2.1 data (2000–2025) using trend tests built for climate data, false-discovery correction, and spatial cluster analysis. On simulated data with no trend, our tests raised false alarms 3–6% of the time, compared with 29–34% for the standard method. The pipeline identified 5.7 million km² of wetting (Central Sahel, northern China) and 4.2 million km² of drying (southern Andes, southwestern Amazon). Where either dataset detects a trend, a second rainfall dataset (CHIRPS) agrees on direction across 87% of that area. The system also exposed its own first result, a global soil-water decline, as an artifact of a documented change in the model’s input data, and we withdrew it. A physics-informed neural network emulates NASA’s land model one month ahead with about 20% lower squared error than a linear baseline. Paradox Earth shows that a stable global average can hide continent-scale regional change, and gives every finding a public report card so anyone can see what is changing, where, and how certain it is.
details:
Earth’s average rainfall over land has not detectably changed in 26 years. Underneath that average, 9.9 million km² of land, an area the size of the United States, is getting significantly wetter or drier. Paradox Earth is an interpretable, human-centered trend detector: it finds those places, maps them, and grades how far each finding can be trusted.

Live explorer: https://paradox-earth.vercel.app/site/ (also at https://paradoxearth.xyz)

Code: https://github.com/kevzho/paradox-earth

The problem

Global averages make the headlines, but water decisions are made region by region. An average can stay flat while one region floods more and another dries out. Existing tools show a trend. They rarely tell a non-expert whether that trend is real.

What we built

Paradox Earth is a geospatial AI and spatial statistics system with three parts.

First, a calibrated trend engine. It tests 17,284 land tiles across 312 months of NASA GLDAS-2.1 data (2000–2025). Natural wet and dry spells trick standard tests into finding trends that are not there. On simulated data with no trend, the standard method we started with raised false alarms 29–34% of the time. Ours does it 3–6% of the time.

Then we implemented spatial statistics that turn scattered tiles into regions. A single significant tile can be chance. We correct for testing thousands of tiles at once (Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery correction), then use local Moran’s I (LISA) with 9,999 random permutations to find places where a trend clusters across neighboring tiles. A region only counts if it is a spatial cluster and statistically significant in the same direction. We then check that it holds under a second definition of “neighbor.”

Finally, we had a physics-informed neural network. We trained a neural network to imitate NASA's land model. It looks at this month's maps of rain, temperature and the water stored on land (in soil, snow and plants), and predicts how that stored water will change next month. During training, it is penalized whenever its prediction breaks the water balance: the change in stored water must equal rain minus evaporation minus runoff. With that rule, its water-balance error dropped by 44%, and its accuracy didn't fall.

Results, in numbers

5.7 million km² show detectable wetting (Central Sahel, northern China, northwest India) and 4.2 million km² show detectable drying (southern Andes, southwestern Amazon, middle Zambezi) over 2000–2025. The shares vary with the time window (2003–2025: 1.3% wetting, 2.6% drying), but all six regions keep their direction in every window.

Six regions get a case file with a four-part report card. Three pass all four checks. The others are graded lower, in plain view.

A second rainfall dataset (CHIRPS, through NASA FLDAS) agrees on the direction of change across 87% of the land area where either dataset detects a trend.

The neural network’s squared errors are 19–22% smaller than a linear model’s, including on a quarter of the globe it never trained on. The physics penalty cuts its water-budget error by 44% (7.5 to 4.2 mm/month) with no loss of accuracy.

In northwest India, satellite gravity (GRACE) shows water storage falling by 204 mm per decade while the land model’s soil water rises. That lines up with groundwater (and possibly glacier) loss the model cannot see.

Catching our own mistakes

Our first headline was a 26-year global decline in soil water. The system’s own checks showed that the decline came mostly from two sudden shifts, timed with documented changes in the data that drive NASA’s model. A comparison with an earlier model version and a second NASA model confirmed it, and we withdrew the result.

Novelty

Spatial statistics as the discovery engine. Most trend tools color a map and leave the reader to spot patterns by eye. Ours tests where change clusters in space: for every tile, LISA asks whether its neighbors are changing the same way more often than chance would allow.

We also have evidence that grades itself. Every finding comes with a four-part report card: does it hold across time windows, across neighbor definitions, in a second rainfall dataset, and in published research? Regions that fail checks are still shown, with their lower grade. We have not seen another public trend explorer that scores its own findings this way.

Before running our tests on NASA data, we ran our tests on thousands of simulated records with no trend. That is how we measured the false-alarm rates above.

Furthermore, we created a self-correcting system. A controlled comparison confirmed the soil-water artifact: the same land model run with different inputs does not show the same shift. Checking a dataset for breaks before trusting its trend is now a built-in step.

The neural network also has to obey the water budget. It is tested on years and a quarter of the globe it never saw, and reported next to the simple model it has to beat. We also show where it fails: when the physics penalty is set too high, accuracy collapses, and we publish that too.

Finally, we integrated three independent lines of NASA evidence in one place. First, a land model (GLDAS), a second model with different rainfall inputs (FLDAS with CHIRPS), and satellite gravity (GRACE) are checked against each other. Where they disagree, as in northwest India, the gap points to water the land model does not track: groundwater, and possibly glacier ice.

Who it helps

Students, teachers, citizen scientists and local planners can open a 3D globe, click a region, and see what is changing, by how much, and how strong the evidence is. Each case file names who could use it, such as an agricultural extension office in the Sahel choosing crop varieties and sowing dates. No code is needed. Every number comes from NASA data, and every claim is statistical, never a claim about cause.

Tools

Python (NumPy, pandas, SciPy, xarray, netCDF4, statsmodels, arch, PySAL, scikit-learn, Matplotlib, earthaccess), PyTorch on a rented RunPod RTX 4090 for the neural network, globe.gl and three.js for the 3D globe, FFmpeg for the video, and Vercel for hosting. The code is open, has 38 automated tests, and reproduces from a free NASA Earthdata login.

What we considered

GLDAS is model output, not direct measurement, so we checked it against other datasets. Results depend on the time window, so we report three. Percent changes look large in dry places, so case files also show absolute amounts. Missing data stays missing.

Use of AI tools

An AI coding assistant helped write and review code, design and run the simulations and neural network experiment, and draft explanatory text. Every number is computed by the code from NASA data.
